items.title: Dawoud Sabu Adeyola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 30, 2025
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] I just was reading a book about early rock & roll and the chitlin’ circuit and how popular guys like Roy Brown were at the time in the mid-50s. I’m wondering if that music... was that something you listened to?

ctx.x: I was. I was, you know I was taking classical lessons, like I say my mother started me at the Wurtlitzer School of Music in downtown Buffalo when I was about eight. And they had a deal going that if you bought a new piano you got a year or two of free lessons with the piano. So me and my big sister, we both availed ourself, and we’d go for lessons. And then after that ran out then my mother hired a piano teacher who came by the house you know. And so we were doing all the regular you know piano primer books, but…

I just was reading a book about early rock & roll and the chitlin’ circuit and how popular guys like Roy Brown were at the time in the mid-50s. I’m wondering if that music, which was — we used to think of it was pre-rock & roll, or R&B, was that something you listened to? And also I wonder what did your parents like having played in the house? What kind of music?

Well first of all people will ask me what drew me to the bass and I tell them I used to spend, my father sang bass in the choir at the church. And as a little guy I used to stand next to him while he was rolling out these luscious bass notes, you know, in the choir. And so the church was full of family members who were involved in music. My aunt played the organ, directed the choir. I had another uncle who was a baritone soloist. He used to do solo concerts. And my cousins, you know they all play. So we just had…
